title: Robin Hood and Dew Drop nightlife, then and now
summary: Clubs were full and safe in the 1940s; fear of crime has driven people to private clubs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well how did the club like the Robin Hood, how did it differ from the city Dewdrop or the Starlight or?

Well the Robin Hood, Paul Gaten was playing at the Robin Hood. See, so this was before Paul Gaten went on Canal Street. And Paul Gaten was very popular, Anna Laura was singing. Singing. And she was very popular, and you know, it just drew its people. Well back then, all the night clubs drew their people then. You see the Robin Hood would be full, and you go around down to Dewdrop, they was full. You know, Armstead's Bar, they had a club right there on Jackson Avenue, what, two blocks from Claiborne, you know, going towards downtown here. They had a club on that corner down there. They had, well back then people frequent night clubs much more than they did because you wasn't afraid to go places. You know, I could leave home from Jefferson, catch the bus and go to town, and have fun, and come home two, three o'clock in the morning hitchhiking or something, and not afraid. But you see, that was then, not now.
You think that's the reason people don't go out?

Well, yeah, definitely. I know this to be a fact, you know, because I know with me, there's certain places I would go and I park where I can hurry up and get back to my car without too much problem. And, and, and, and, and, and, and, and the places I go, I'll be watching and looking, you know, because I'm, this is just the way it is, this is a sign of the time and it's bad. You see, and it's bad for everybody because the people that have money in their pocket, that's why they have so many private places now. And I, like the Autocrat Club, as an example. Now do you know, Ted, you ought to go up there sometimes. You know, I've. I know, I mean I know the place.
